title: How to Read Uneven Tire Wear Patterns (A Visual Guide)
body_html:
How to Read Uneven Tire Wear Patterns (A Visual Guide)

Uneven tire wear is your tires talking. Each pattern points to a specific cause — overinflation, alignment, a worn suspension component, or a wheel that needs balancing. Once you know how to read the signs, you can catch problems before they turn into a flat on Deerfoot or a surprise bill at the shop.

The patterns below are the most common ones we see at Prince Tires in Calgary. Most are easy to spot during a five-minute walkaround — no lift required.

The Short Version

  • Center wear — overinflation
  • Edge wear (both shoulders) — underinflation
  • One-sided wear — alignment or camber issue
  • Cupping / scalloping — worn suspension or out-of-balance wheel
  • Feathering — toe misalignment
  • Flat spots / patchy wear — hard braking, cold-storage, or balance issue

1. Center Wear — Overinflation

If the middle strip of tread is worn faster than both edges, the tire is carrying too much pressure. Overinflated tires balloon out in the centre and ride on a narrow contact strip instead of the full tread width — that strip takes all the abuse.

Calgary summers amplify this. Tire pressure rises roughly 1 PSI for every 6°C of temperature increase. Set your pressures on a cold January morning and ignore them through a hot August, and you can end up 5–6 PSI overinflated without noticing. Check pressure monthly using the spec on your driver's door jamb, not the maximum rating stamped on the sidewall.

2. Edge Wear (Both Shoulders) — Underinflation

Both outer edges worn more than the centre means underinflation. Low pressure lets the sidewalls flex excessively, causing the shoulders to carry extra load.

This is the most common pattern we see. Calgary's chinook cycles — rapid temperature swings of 15–20°C in a single day — can drop tire pressure by 3–4 PSI overnight. Check and adjust every 3–4 weeks, especially through spring and fall. Edge wear from chronic underinflation also stresses the sidewall and shortens the overall life of the tire.

3. One-Sided Wear — Camber or Alignment

When only one edge of a tire is worn — inner or outer — the wheel is not sitting perfectly vertical. Negative camber (top of the tire leaning inward) grinds the inner edge; positive camber does the opposite on the outer edge.

Calgary's pothole season, running roughly late March through May, knocks vehicles out of alignment more than almost any other time of year. One solid hit can shift things enough to noticeably wear a tire over the following months. A tire rotation at Prince Tires often surfaces this — we will let you know which corner is the problem so you can get alignment addressed.

4. Cupping and Scalloping — Suspension or Balance Issue

Cupping looks like a series of dips or scooped-out sections carved into the tread all the way around the tire — not a flat spot in one place, but a wavy, rhythmic pattern. It happens when a tire bounces on the road rather than rolling smoothly, usually from worn shocks or struts, or from a significantly out-of-balance wheel.

Cupping is easier to feel than see. A rhythmic thud or vibration at highway speeds on the QE2 or Stoney Trail is a common indicator. For the balance side of this problem, wheel balancing at Prince Tires resolves vibration from an unbalanced wheel. Worn shocks and struts are a suspension repair outside our scope — those need to be addressed first so the tire stops cupping.

5. Feathering — Toe Misalignment

Feathering is subtle and often missed on a visual check. The tread blocks develop a sharp edge on one side and a rounded edge on the other, like a row of shark fins. Run your palm across the tread from the inside edge to the outside — if it feels sharper one way than the other, you have feathering.

It is caused by toe misalignment: the tires are not pointing exactly straight ahead. Curb strikes, worn tie rod ends, and Calgary road wear all contribute. Alignment correction (done at a shop that handles that service) fixes the root cause. A follow-up rotation at Prince Tires helps redistribute any wear that has already accumulated.

6. Flat Spots and Patchy Wear — Braking or Cold Storage

A flat spot is a worn section in one location on the circumference. Hard braking without ABS can scrub a flat spot in seconds. Cold-weather storage is the other common cause — a vehicle left parked for weeks in a Calgary winter can develop temporary flat spots where the tires sat on frozen concrete.

For cold-storage flat spots, gradual driving for the first 20–30 km usually works them out. For braking-related flat spots, have the tire inspected — the damage may be cosmetic or it may be too deep. If your TPMS warning light is on alongside unusual wear, our TPMS sensor services page covers what we can do. A slow leak causes uneven loading that accelerates wear over time, so a blinking TPMS light is worth addressing, not ignoring.

How to Inspect Your Own Tires in 5 Minutes

You do not need special tools. A walkaround takes about five minutes:

  1. Crouch down and look across the tread face — check that wear is even from the inner edge to the outer edge.
  2. Run your palm across the tread width — sharp edges or wavy surfaces tell you more than your eyes alone.
  3. Use a toonie for depth — insert it into the main groove. If you can see above the bear's paws, you have around 4/32" remaining. Start planning a replacement at that point.
  4. Compare all four tires — one outlier almost always points to a problem at that corner of the vehicle.
  5. Check when you last rotated — most manufacturers recommend every 8,000–12,000 km. A seasonal changeover is a natural rotation point.

Calgary-Specific Wear Triggers

A few things unique to Calgary that speed up uneven wear:

  • Pothole season (March–May): Alignment hits and flat-spot risks peak here. Inspect your tires after any hard impact.
  • Chinook pressure swings: A 20°C temperature swing overnight can drop tire pressure by 3–4 PSI, leading to shoulder wear if left unchecked.
  • Mountain driving: Hwy 1 switchbacks put extra lateral load on outside edges. Worth a look after a Banff or Canmore trip.
  • Winter tires left on too long: Soft-compound winter tires wear their centres quickly on hot summer pavement. Swap by late April.
  • The late-October booking rush: Calgary's first significant snowfall typically arrives in mid-to-late October. Book your seasonal changeover a few weeks early to avoid waiting.

FAQ: Tire Wear Patterns

My tires look fine but I feel a vibration at highway speed. Could it be wear?

Cupping or scalloping is hard to see but easy to feel. A rhythmic vibration that worsens at a specific speed — often 90–110 km/h on the highway — is a common sign. Run your hand across the tread to check for dips around the circumference. A wheel balance check will confirm whether the vibration is wear-related or a straightforward balance issue. If the balance checks out and the vibration doesn't, road force balancing can tell whether one tire is out of round.

How often should Calgary drivers rotate their tires?

Every 8,000–12,000 km is the standard guideline. If you swap between summer and winter tires seasonally, each changeover is a natural rotation opportunity — ask the Prince Tires team to include it at your next booking. Consistent rotation is one of the best things you can do to get even wear across all four tires and extend their life.

Can I fix alignment-related wear by just rotating the tires?

Not really. Rotation moves tires to new positions, but if alignment is still off, the new position will just develop a different wear pattern. Fix the alignment first, then rotate — otherwise you're spreading damage rather than preventing it. Prince Tires handles rotation; alignment needs to go to a shop that handles mechanical repairs.

I only have wear on the inside edge. Is it safe to drive?

Inside-edge wear from negative camber means less rubber is in contact with the road than there should be. That shortens your braking distance and reduces wet-weather grip. It is worth getting looked at sooner rather than later — we can assess the tires and tell you where you stand.
